rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cave-dwellers passage answers an objection from the Prophet’s opponents and presents their real story without needless details.
rows.anchor: their real life aside from needless details becomes evident

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The youths’ trials parallel the Prophet and his companions’ preaching phase; perseverance brings God’s easing of hardship and provision, and He does not let His persevering servants lose their way.
rows.anchor: God will ease out their hardships the way He did so for them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet should attend to poor companions and disregard people enslaved by worldly wealth.
rows.anchor: focus his attention to his poor and indigent companions while disregarding those who have become slaves to the wealth of this world

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Though poor in worldly goods, the companions abound in faith and devote themselves to remembrance and spreading religion.
rows.anchor: they have the wealth of faith in abundance

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is told not to grieve over unbelievers: if they refuse faith, they will face God’s established, unchangeable practice.
rows.anchor: They will be dealt with according to the established practice of God and no one can change this practice

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The worldly-life similitude addresses people who take worldly success as proof that their beliefs are right and assume they will remain successful in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: They regard their worldly successes to be a proof that it is they who are following the right path

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The similitude teaches that worldly pleasures pass away, while righteous deeds alone accompany people to the next life.
rows.anchor: Only their righteous deeds will go with them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account of Adam and Satan warns arrogant Quraysh that their evil has made Satan, Adam’s open enemy, their guardian.
rows.anchor: they have made Satan and his progeny their friends and guardians

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God sent a Book that explains truth in many ways, yet Quraysh stubbornly demand to see the threatened punishment.
rows.anchor: instead of accepting it, these people became adamant in their demand to show them a sign of the punishment

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses’ journey trains him in patience by teaching that events occur under God’s wise will, even when human beings cannot grasp the reasons.
rows.anchor: whatever happens in this world happens with God’s will and this will is entirely based on wisdom

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account teaches the Prophet and believers not to be cowed by rebellious people prospering while truth-seekers suffer; they should persist and await God’s wisdom.
rows.anchor: they should not be over-awed and scared to see the rebellious and the defiant spreading mischief

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ship’s damage among poor people and repair of a collapsing wall in an oppressors’ city illustrate wisdom humans cannot perceive.
rows.anchor: if in this world a hole is drilled in the ship of the poor, there is great wisdom in it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dhu al-Qarnayn is presented as a just ruler and lesson for Quraysh: despite vast conquests, he credited his victories to God, unlike Quraysh’s arrogance over limited political power.
rows.anchor: even after conquering all the territories of the east and the west, he regarded all his victories to be a blessing of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The concluding section returns to the warning that opened the sūrah, restating its central theme in a new style.
rows.anchor: The topic of warning is once again brought up with which the sūrah began

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closing answer to mockery of the Qur’an and demands for miracles points to countless divine signs within and around people.
rows.anchor: if oceans become ink, even then they cannot all be penned

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet declares that signs and miracles belong to God alone; he is God’s servant and recites what is revealed.
rows.anchor: showing signs and miracles is the prerogative of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This overview is offered as sufficient to establish the sūrah’s coherence and central theme before its detailed exegesis.
rows.anchor: This concise analysis of the meanings of the sūrah is sufficient to explain its coherence and central theme

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah begins with the same subject as the preceding sūrah’s conclusion.
rows.anchor: This sūrah begins with the same topic on which the previous sūrah ended

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Arabs owe gratitude for the Qur’an, but instead some fail to value this favour and invent excuses to deny it.
rows.anchor: show gratitude and not otherwise. Unfortunate are the people who are not valuing this favour

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an is free of ambiguity in text and meaning, lucid Arabic, and guides to the straight path through arguments found in human nature, intellect and the world.
rows.anchor: It guides people to the straight path

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The object after “to warn” may be understood as the deniers, with the suppressed phrase indicated by the later parallel mention of believers.
rows.anchor: the word ﻟﻠْ or ﻟﻠْﻤﻜَﺬ	ﺑ:> is suppressed as evidenced by the parallel mention

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The subject of “warn” can be God, who revealed the Book to warn disbelievers of severe punishment.
rows.anchor: the meaning would be that God has revealed this specially from Himself to inform the disbelievers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the subject can be the Prophet, who conveys divine punishment; “from Him” then stresses its intensity.
rows.anchor: the meaning would be that God’s messenger informs people of divine punishment

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Wherein they abide forever” refers to Paradise, naming the consequence while mentioning the reward, a common Arabic style.
rows.anchor: They actually refer to Paradise

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The mention of those who claim God has begotten a child specifies a case within the general warning, especially idolaters and Christians.
rows.anchor: The last of the above mentioned verses is a mention of the specific after the general

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Knowledge” means conclusive proof: those who attribute children or partners to God have neither divine sanction nor evidence and blindly follow their ancestors.
rows.anchor: The word “knowledge” here means “conclusive proof.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Attributing children to God is a false, gravely disrespectful accusation, and the people will soon face its consequence if they persist.
rows.anchor: It is a false accusation on God and a matter of grave disrespect to Him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning to the Prophet is affectionate; it restrains his grief and exhausting effort, since rejection is not caused by obscurity in the Book or a failure in his preaching.
rows.anchor: he should not go overboard in discharging his duty

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The earth’s adornment is a test of who uses reason to seek the Hereafter and who follows desire in seeking worldly life.
rows.anchor: This world is a place of trial and test

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Worldly pleasures and status are immediately available while their pains are hidden; Hereafter’s successes remain unseen and pursuing them brings worldly hardships, making this a severe test.
rows.anchor: All its pleasures are at hand and easy to attain while its pains are hidden

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Only perceptive people resist worldly lures rather than sacrifice the Hereafter’s blessings for them.
rows.anchor: Only those will sail through it who are perspicacious enough not to be misled by these worldly lures

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word “juruza” means barren land; the world’s attractions are temporary and God will destroy them, as discussed further in verses 46–48.
rows.anchor: The word ﺟﺮز refers to barren land

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cave-dwellers question was planted by the People of the Book and posed by Quraysh to harass and corner the Prophet, not to seek truth.
rows.anchor: These irrelevant questions were obviously not meant to find out the real truth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Opponents planned to exploit either an inability to answer or an answer conflicting with their own beliefs.
rows.anchor: if the Prophet (sws) was able to answer them and the answer was against their beliefs

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an generally counsels ignoring such questions, but answers when useful; the truthful account both answers and trains the Prophet and companions in perseverance during comparable trials.
rows.anchor: if some question is beneficial or its answer can be beneficial for education

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an preserves the useful, true part of the cave story, correcting false accretions and restoring a major chapter in truth-seekers’ history.
rows.anchor: a very important chapter in the history of the seekers of the truth was cleansed from all sorts of wrong details

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The dwellers’ identities, date and ancestry cannot be known securely; beyond the Qur’anic account, claims are folk tales, and further inquiry is discouraged.
rows.anchor: Who were the cave-dwellers, when did they inhabit the earth and whose ancestors were they are questions that cannot be answered with certainty

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi’s opinion is that the youths were ancestors of Christians, not Quraysh or Jews, and belonged to the early Christian period under Roman persecution.
rows.anchor: in my opinion, they belonged to the initial period of the Christians when they were persecuted by the Romans

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He says they boldly preached monotheism and accountability, faced imminent stoning, then took refuge in a cave where God supplied extraordinary protection.
rows.anchor: They fearlessly invited people to monotheism and warned them of the accountability in the hereafter

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After their circumstances became known, groups built memorials and claimed them; Christian retellings gradually reduced their story to miracles and unsupported details.
rows.anchor: Gradually, this tradition became confined to some miraculous feats and baseless details about them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Debates over their number and dog obscured their message and sacrifices; Islahi says the true history was later lost as Christianity’s teachings were distorted.
rows.anchor: no one knew what their real message was and the extent of sacrifices they gave

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Distorted reports about the youths circulated among Arab Christians, who prompted the question; the Qur’an answered to reassure the Prophet and companions in adversity.
rows.anchor: he could receive great assurance and strength in the adverse circumstances he and his companions were passing through

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The youths’ persecution and cave refuge parallel the Prophet and companions’ trials and their coming migrations to Abyssinia, the Thawr cave and Madinah.
rows.anchor: the Prophet (sws) and his companions too had to face tremendous trials at the hands of the Quraysh

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi holds that the opening question addresses the question-raisers generally, not the Prophet, since he learned the story through revelation and had no reason to wonder at it.
rows.anchor: In my opinion, this question is addressed to the people who had raised this issue

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A singular address may target each member of a group, like “Did you not see?”, and can carry stronger emphasis than a plural address.
rows.anchor: has more emphasis in it than a plural address

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The singular forms in verses 17 and 18 are likewise addressed to individuals in a group rather than the Prophet.
rows.anchor: in this very section (see verses 17 and 18), there are instances in which the addressed entity is singular

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The questioners used the cave story to diminish the Prophet and companions, arguing that earlier holy people had divine signs while the new religion lacked a foundation.
rows.anchor: past for whom such divine signs of splendour manifested themselves

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cave-dwellers are one sign among many; God controls such signs across time, and no group has exclusive possession of them.
rows.anchor: This was just one sign among numerous other signs of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, if the address is to the Prophet, the verse says the event is not uniquely strange; earlier and future signs promise God’s protection for him and his companions.
rows.anchor: if someone regards the verse to address the Prophet (sws), then in that case, it would mean

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Cave” identifies the youths because they took refuge there; this was their title among the People of the Book in Arabia.
rows.anchor: Their ascription to al-kahf obviously is because they took refuge in the cave

rows.speaker: Ka‘b
rows.claim: In a report through ‘Ikrimah from Ibn ‘Abbas, Ka‘b identifies al-raqīm as the city from which the youths came, also called the valley of raqīm.
rows.anchor: in the opinion of Ka‘b (rta), it was the name of a city from which these youngsters had come out

rows.speaker: some researchers of current times
rows.claim: Some modern researchers identify al-raqīm with Petra, called Batrā by Arabs.
rows.anchor: Some researchers of current times think that this is the name of the city which was famous by the name of Petra

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Finding the origin of an Arabicized non-Arabic place-name is virtually impossible and has no educational utility.
rows.anchor: finding out their original names is virtually impossible and this does not have any utility for the purpose of eduction either

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb rashada means to be guided and granted steadfastness; the expression about one’s affair means guidance in that matter.
rows.anchor: The verb رَشَدَ means that he was guided and bestowed with steadfastness
